newsitem.title: FRANCE: Judges to probe fraud allegations at French bank.
newsitem.headline: Judges to probe fraud allegations at French bank.

text.p: A Paris prosecutor appointed two investigating magistrates on Tuesday to probe allegations of fraud at Credit Lyonnais in a bid to seek those responsible for one of the biggest financial scandals in French banking history.
Justice sources identified the judges who will investigate the huge losses run up by the state-owned bank in the early 1990s as Eva Joly and Jean-Pierre Zanoto.
The pair are well acquainted with the bank as they are already investigating key subsidiaries which made some of its most controversial loans during the late 1980s and early 1990s.
While more than 40 judicial inquiries are under way into the activities of Credit Lyonnais's units, there has never been a legal investigation into the parent bank.
The bank was brought to the brink of collapse by the massive losses that stemmed from runaway expansion.

The investigation follows calls by Finance Minister Jean Arthuis last August for legal action over alleged irregularities in the bank's accounts when Socialist-appointed Jean-Yves Haberer was its chairman.

Arthuis said he wanted to bring former senior managers to justice for failing to keep control of subsidiaries during an expansion spree which briefly transformed Credit Lyonnais into the largest bank outside Japan.
Under Haberer, the bank went on a dash for growth, acquiring a big array of expensive assets and loans that went sour.
Haberer was dismissed by the government and later replaced by Jean Peyrelevade.

The parent bank was investigated by a parliamentary commission which concluded in 1994 that "nothing could be reproached to Jean-Yves Haberer in terms of ethics, honesty and honour", although it said he bore responsibility for some misguided decisions.

Arthuis's call for the investigation last summer rattled financial markets which worried it could engulf Bank of France governor Jean-Claude Trichet, who headed the Treasury and was in charge of supervising banks in the early 1990s.

Arthuis said later Trichet was in no way targeted but French media commentators have suggested a judicial investigation would inevitably mean examination of the effectiveness of the government's financial supervisory activities.
The French media has also suggested that Arthuis' call for an investigation was politically timed to soften up the public for a third state bailout of Credit Lyonnais.

The bank, which reported losses of 21 billion francs between 1992 and 1994, has been rescued twice by the government. A third rescue is expected soon to bolster its balance sheet and pave the way for its privatisation.
The total cost to French taxpayers from the bank's lending escapades could total more than 100 billion francs, some press reports have suggested.
